entry.title: Recognise a lesson by the recording its card plays, and read past a n…
entry.content:
Recognise a lesson by the recording its card plays, and read past a note that is gone

Reviewing #8 (ad17fc9) against the learner's own collection turned up a wrong
claim, two crashes, and a better identifier than the one the ticket was built
on.

The claim first, because it is the one that mattered: ADR-0009 said the cards it
could not recognise belonged to lessons the tool cannot build yet. They do not.
Matching the learner's 102 hand-made cards to lessons by the dialogue recording
each card plays shows every one of them is for a lesson the tool builds, and 54
of them are for one it builds today. The measurement behind the claim was a
prefix comparison, which a single differing word early in a dialogue destroys;
the audio field names the lesson outright, and nothing about a card's wording
can spoil it. The ADR's numbers are corrected, and the README and CONTEXT say
what was measured rather than what was guessed.

That identification is worth having in the tool, not only in the measurement.
Import now looks for a note playing the lesson's dialogue recording before it
compares any words: the audio is attached under the filename the corpus gave it,
no two lessons were recorded into one file, and a hand-made card's own text may
depart from the corpus's by a word or two -- `religous` for `religious`,
`daughter` for `son` -- without the lesson being a different lesson. Matching
the words more loosely was the alternative and is rejected: a rule for comparing
words that could call those the same could just as easily call another lesson's
the same. Measured against the collection: `181 imported, 102 left as they
were, 82 skipped`, every one of the 102 recognised, where the tag-and-words rule
alone left 54 of them to be duplicated.

Two failures the review found in the reading of the deck. AnkiConnect answers an
empty object for a note id that is gone, which is what a run meets if a note is
deleted or synced away between the search and the read; subscripting it raised a
KeyError that no part of the command line catches, so a corpus-wide run would
have died in a traceback with no summary and nothing said about where. The run
reads past such an answer now, and the stub can put a collection in that state,
which it could not before. The other: a note was indexed by its dialogue only if
it carried no `englishpod::` tag, so a lesson whose code changed under it --
re-read from another document, or corrected by hand -- was recognised by neither
its tag nor its words, though ADR-0009 and the README both promise tag *or*
words. Every note is read for all three now.

And one the review found in the escape handling: a lesson whose text layer
prints `"` reaches its card as `&quot;`, and a hand-made card of the
same dialogue holds the character itself, so the two were compared as
`quotEdquot` against `Ed`. Entities are resolved until they settle, which is
what a card carrying the lesson's words rather than the extraction's escapes
needs.

Tests, one per finding: a card recognised by the recording it plays and one
playing another lesson's recording that is not a match, a note that vanishes
between the search and the read, a note whose tag names another code, and a card
that spells out what the corpus printed as an entity.

Refs #8.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Ask about a lesson the collection already holds, and refresh it in place
entry.content:
Ask about a lesson the collection already holds, and refresh it in place

Import used to find out that a lesson was already in the collection the hard
way: it added the note, Anki refused it as a duplicate, and the run stopped
there. That left the learner's decision unmade in the one place it matters most,
since the note already there may be one they have studied for months, and a
corpus-wide re-run is where it would bite hardest.

It now reads the deck before it writes a note and asks: leave that note exactly
as it is, or refresh its content and keep everything else about it. One answer
can be given for every lesson left -- `s all`, `r all` -- so a corpus-wide
re-run is a single decision rather than three hundred, and `--existing skip` or
`--existing replace` answers ahead of time, so a scripted run never stalls on a
prompt. A run with nobody to answer and no flag says what it was asked and what
to pass rather than sitting on the question.

Replace is `updateNoteFields` on the note that is there, and nothing else. It is
never a deletion and a note made again: Anki's ids and guids are not
reproducible by the tool (ADR-0004), and a note made again is a card the learner
has never studied in place of one they have -- which would cost exactly the
review history the question exists to protect. A test asserts the note id, the
deck, the tags and the card's scheduling come through a replace unchanged.

A lesson counts as already there by its note's tag, and failing that by its
dialogue. The second is what makes this worth anything for a collection that
predates the tool: the learner's profile holds 102 EnglishPod cards made by hand
that carry no tags at all, so a tag search alone would call every one of them
absent and hand them a second card. What two cards from one lesson share is the
words -- a hand-made card blanks seven of lesson 108's thirteen terms where the
tool blanks eleven, breaks its lines where it likes and punctuates its own way
(`Dont` for `Don't`, `....` for `. . . .`, `partlycloudy` for `partly-cloudy`),
so the comparison takes the blanks, the line breaks and the punctuation out of
both. Measured against the learner's collection, 48 of the 102 are recognised;
the rest are lessons the tool cannot build yet -- the image-only scans above all
-- or five whose card was edited to different words, which import a second card
(ADR-0009 records the count and what it costs).

Two things are reported rather than decided: a lesson the collection holds
twice, since which note is the lesson's is not the tool's to guess, and a note
found by its dialogue whose note type would not render the card, checked exactly
as the tool's own note type is (ADR-0005). Both name the lesson in the run's
summary and leave the others alone.

A lesson left as it is counts as work, so a `--existing skip` run over a corpus
that already holds every lesson exits zero and says how many were left, where a
run that skipped every lesson for reasons of its own still exits non-zero
(ADR-0006, amended).

End to end against the real corpus with a stub holding the learner's 102 notes:
`import: 365 lessons: 235 imported, 48 left as they were, 82 skipped`, 475
requests to the collection and not one of them a write to a note that was
already there.

Tests: the stub holds the notes a test puts in it -- with per-name note types,
since the learner's collection has more than the one this tool makes -- and
answers findNotes, notesInfo and updateNoteFields, so each mode is driven
through the command line and a replace is shown to keep the scheduling it found.
run_cli feeds standard input, empty by default, so a prompt nobody meant to
raise reads an end of file instead of a terminal.

Closes #8.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Pass over an unreadable batch PDF, and keep a title's walk back in bo…
entry.content:
Pass over an unreadable batch PDF, and keep a title's walk back in bounds

Reviewing the batch PDF fallback (de88b23) turned up two things the code should
have done differently, four tests it was missing, and three sentences in the
docs that were not true of it.

A PDF beside the lesson that could not be read at all aborted the search, and
the failure it raised named that file rather than the lesson: a corrupt or
scanned file in the batch directory -- a shape the corpus has elsewhere, in the
69 lessons that want the OCR pass -- would have cost every code-less lesson in
that batch its card with a reason about somebody else's file. Every candidate is
tried now, an unreadable one is passed over in silence, and what went wrong with
one is reported only when none of them carries the lesson after all.

The walk back over a title's first line was bounded by nothing but the top of
the document, so a code row close under another could have produced a slice
beginning before the previous lesson's -- which `_lesson_beside` would have
taken for a lesson and reported as carrying no code. The bound is the previous
lesson's code row now, which makes an empty slice impossible as well as an
overlapping one, and the caller asks a slice to be not empty rather than merely
not absent.

The docs: ADR-0008 promised that a lesson gaining a PDF of its own would end up
with two Markdown files to reconcile, which the code has never done -- the
Markdown a directory holds is the one a re-run writes to, and a test says so. It
said twenty lessons "print a title that way" where the measurement is that
twenty print the row carrying their code apart from the row their title begins
on, fourteen under a wrapped title and six under a one-line one; and it blamed
the column shift in 0282 and 0297 on per-lesson PDFs, which neither lesson has.
It also counted a batch's lessons as always ten, where the corpus's last batch
holds five and its fixture two. The README's example skip line named a file the
corpus does not have, and read a first-run count as though the corpus were
empty, which after a run it is not.

Tests, one per finding: a scanned PDF is not sent looking beside the lesson, an
unreadable PDF beside it is passed over, whichever PDF beside it carries the
lesson supplies it, `--force` keeps the name a recovered lesson's Markdown
already holds, and a directory not named by a number is reported as it was.
Measured against the corpus after the change: all 115 lessons above 250 recover,
twenty of them by walking back over a title's first line, with no empty slice
and none that reaches into the lesson before.

Refs #10.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Read a lesson from its batch's PDF when it has none of its own
entry.content:
Read a lesson from its batch's PDF when it has none of its own

Seventy-seven lessons -- every one of them above 250 -- keep a one-page
introduction sheet where a lesson's PDF would be: it names the lesson and says
what it is about, and carries no lesson code, no dialogue and no vocabulary, so
preprocess skipped all of them and none could ever become a card. Their content
is in the combined PDF one directory up, which is a lesson PDF ten times over:
ten lessons, each beginning at the row that prints its own code, each with a
dialogue and both vocabulary tables.

The stage reads them from there now. A lesson whose own PDF carries no lesson
code is looked for beside it, by the four digits its directory is named with,
one level up only -- that being the batch directory the corpus keeps. The
number says which lesson is wanted; the code the card is identified by is still
read from inside the document the lesson is found in, so a misnamed directory
cannot misname a note. A PDF the stage cannot read at all is not sent looking:
a scan wants the OCR pass, and says so.

Deciding where one lesson ends and the next begins is where the care went. The
marker is the row carrying the code, but a title too long for its column prints
on two rows with the code beside the second -- so the title's first row belongs
to the lesson before the one it names, and since a title row spans the width of
a vocabulary table, a stray one flattens that table's columns into a single
cell. Twenty of the corpus's 115 lessons above 250 print their titles that way,
and slicing at the code row damaged 101 table rows; measured against the
corpus, walking back over a title's first line leaves every lesson's dialogue
identical and swallows no row of any table.

The Markdown lands in the lesson's own directory, named for the code it was
read from (0251/englishpod_C0251.md), and the Markdown a directory already
holds is the one a re-run writes to however it is named -- so --force
regenerates it in place instead of leaving a second file beside it, which is
what used to happen to a hand-renamed one. Measured on the corpus: preprocess
now writes 296 of 365 lessons and skips the 69 image-only scans, where it wrote
219 and skipped 146; build makes 283 notes, two of the recovered lessons short
of the count because their own tables print shifted by a column (0282, 0297) and
the run says so rather than guessing.

ADR-0008 records the decision and what it costs; CONTEXT.md gains Batch PDF and
Introduction sheet beside a Lesson code entry that draws the line between the
number a directory is named with and the code read inside the document; ADR-0006
no longer cites these lessons as a reason a run cannot fix something.

Tested through the command line against a batch fixture drawn the way the
sample lesson PDFs are -- two lessons in one document, the second beginning
mid-page under a wrapped title, which is the case that used to take the first
lesson's columns with it -- plus the corpus-level run that turns a recovered
lesson into a note.

Closes #10.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Report an unreadable ignore file, and match entries whatever the root is
entry.content:
Report an unreadable ignore file, and match entries whatever the root is

Reviewing the ignore file added in 3f397aa against the standard the rest of the
tool meets turned up two ways it could fail its owner.

The file is the one thing a person hand-writes, and a file that is not UTF-8 --
GBK is plausible for a corpus whose directories are named in Chinese -- raised a
UnicodeDecodeError out of the stage and killed the run with a traceback. It is
now reported the way every other unreadable thing is: the run stops and says
which file it cannot read. A UTF-8 byte-order mark, which some editors write by
default, no longer disables the first entry in silence; the file is read as
utf-8-sig.

An absolute entry now names the same directory when the corpus is given to a
stage as a relative path, which it did not: the entry was resolved against the
root only when the root was absolute, so `build corpus` with the absolute path
its owner had in front of them excluded nothing, while the README and ADR-0007
both said it would. Both sides are resolved before they are compared, and an
entry opening with `./` is normalised now too.

The rest of the review's findings are in the words rather than the code. An
entry naming a batch directory prunes it before anything asks what it is, so it
takes its ten lessons and the combined PDF that would otherwise have been
reported in their place out of the run in silence -- stated in the README and
ADR-0007 rather than left implied. The README now gives the comment rule, since
it is what makes a directory whose name opens with `#` unnameable. ADR-0007 had
the host-transcript directory in the family it has since been moved out of, and
CONTEXT.md had the file at "the corpus root" where the code reads it at whatever
root a stage is pointed at. In the code, `excluded` became `ignored`, the
glossary's word for the thing, and `corpus.py`'s module docstring no longer
claims the layout is the only list there is.

Tests cover both bugs and the hazard: an absolute entry under a relative root, a
byte-order mark, a file that cannot be decoded, an entry naming a batch
directory, and the case the previous test only appeared to cover -- a lesson
named in the ignore file beside it is still the lesson when a stage is pointed
straight at it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Leave a directory out of a corpus run
entry.content:
Leave a directory out of a corpus run

A corpus holds material that belongs to no lesson, and the walk could not tell:
`英语博客51-100/ENGLISHPOD主持人对话文本/` holds 178 host-transcript PDFs, so
every run found it, could not choose a file from it, and reported it as one
more skipped lesson. The corpus's owner can now name such a directory in
`.englishpodignore`, at the root a stage is pointed at, by its own name or by
its path from that root, and the walk neither descends into it nor reports it.
Measured on the real corpus, the summary goes from 366 lessons to 365 and the
line naming that directory is gone.

Matching is exact -- a name or a path, never a glob or a prefix -- because the
two directions fail differently: an entry that over-matches takes lessons out
of every run and says nothing about it, while an entry that matches nothing
excludes nothing and the directory it named comes back to the report. That
same asymmetry is what keeps this from being the hand-maintained list ADR-0006
rejects: a lesson list goes stale by silently omitting lessons that exist, an
exclusion list by loudly excluding none. ADR-0007 records the exception;
CONTEXT.md gains `Ignored directory` beside `Skipped lesson`, which nothing
about this declines, and the README's measured example moves to the steady
state with a section of its own for the file.

An explicit path is not discovery: pointing a stage at an ignored directory
still works. Excluding every lesson of a batch leaves the batch directory
holding its combined PDF with no lesson beneath it, which is what a lesson
directory looks like, so it is reported as one in their place -- visible, and
the honest shape of a corpus whose lessons someone has put out of the tool's
sight.

Tested through the command line: the name and path forms, an absolute path
with a trailing slash, comments and blank lines, a stale entry that changes
nothing, a lesson still worked on when its directory is named directly, and
the batch promotion above.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Report a PDF that cannot be opened, and correct the corpus numbers
entry.content:
Report a PDF that cannot be opened, and correct the corpus numbers

Reviewing the change against the ticket turned up two things worth fixing.

A file that is not a PDF at all raised pdfminer's error through the stage
and out of the run: a traceback, and every lesson after it abandoned --
which is what "one malformed lesson never stops the run" exists to forbid.
The reader now raises the error the other unreadable lessons raise, so a
corrupt file is one skipped lesson named in the summary, and a stage pointed
at it says what is wrong rather than printing where the library gave up.
pdfplumber wraps both a failed open and a failed page in its own exception,
which is the net drawn here; nothing reaches past it into pdfminer. Tests
cover the corrupt file both in a corpus run and on its own.

The README's corpus example was invented rather than measured, and was
wrong. The real corpus preprocesses 217 lessons and skips 149, so it now
carries the measured counts and says what the 149 are -- 69 image-only scans
that want the OCR pass, 77 lesson-introduction sheets that carry no lesson
code in the batches above 250, 3 directories holding more than one PDF --
since that is what a first run should be read against. Measured as well: a
build over those 217 makes 206 cards and skips 160, six of them for a
missing dialogue recording and five for a Key Vocabulary table with no
entries to blank.

The ADR also records the quiet edge of the rule that reads a directory
holding lessons as a container: a lesson directory that ever gains a
subdirectory holding lesson files becomes a container, and the lesson is
then neither built nor skipped nor named. No directory in the corpus is
shaped that way, and the alternative rule reads each batch's combined PDF as
one more lesson, which is the likelier harm.

Refs #5.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Run a stage over the whole corpus
entry.content:
Run a stage over the whole corpus

Each stage now takes either one lesson directory or the corpus directory
holding them, and works out which it was given from what the path holds: a
stage pointed at the corpus works through every lesson in it, and ends with
a summary of the ones it skipped.

The corpus has no index of its lessons, so its layout is the index -- and
the layout is not uniform. The first families keep one lesson a directory
and the later ones nest ten, each batch directory carrying a combined PDF
of its ten beside the lesson directories, so a directory is a lesson when it
holds a lesson's files (its PDF, its recordings, its Markdown) and holds no
lesson beneath it. That second half is what keeps the combined PDF from
becoming a lesson of its own. It is also why 0001 and 0164 -- the lessons
with no dialogue audio -- are found at all, and reported once their Markdown
is there.

A lesson that cannot be read, or that cannot make a card, is skipped and
named in the stage's own words rather than emitted as a degraded card, and
one malformed lesson never stops the run. Build now refuses a lesson whose
dialogue carries none of its Key Vocabulary: a note with nothing blanked
looks complete in the collection and asks the learner nothing. What does
stop a run is the collection itself -- an Anki that cannot be reached, a
missing deck, a note type that is not the card's design, a note refused --
and it stops where that happened, saying how many notes had landed, since
half a corpus imported is worse than none. That is the current answer to a
lesson already in the collection too, until #8 asks rather than decides.

A run that worked on no lesson at all exits non-zero even though no lesson
failed on its own, so a script cannot mistake it for success. Skipped
lessons are reported together at the end. The message for an ambiguous
directory now names three of its files and counts the rest, because one
corpus directory holds 178 of them and a run over the corpus reports it.

ADR-0006 records the decisions and the cost: a run can succeed while
looking incomplete, and the summary grows with the corpus.

Tested through the command line against a corpus fixture laid out the way
the real one is -- a lesson and a malformed lesson a directory deep, a
batch directory carrying a combined PDF, one lesson missing its dialogue
audio, and something that is not a lesson at all -- plus a corpus of PDFs
for preprocess. The stub AnkiConnect now answers for a note type it was
asked to create, which a run over a corpus asks of the second note on.

Closes #5.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Refuse a note type that is not the card's design
entry.content:
Refuse a note type that is not the card's design

Import creates `EnglishPod Cloze` when the collection lacks it, and until
now adopted one already there as it stood. Reading the learner's own
collection showed why that is wrong: their profile holds an EnglishPod
Cloze with the six fields in the right order and a card that renders only
`Sentences` and `Phonetic symbols` -- a note type started by hand and never
finished. Notes added to it would carry a glossary and a dialogue
recording that no card ever shows, and Anki reports nothing when it
happens: a field the note type lacks is dropped from a note in silence.

Import now reads the note type's fields and its card sides and compares
them with the design before writing anything. A missing field, a card side
that never renders a field the design renders, or a note type making more
than one card a note stops the run with what differs named. The check is
deliberately narrow: extra fields, restyling and the order the back
renders them are the learner's, and only content decides.

Repairing the note type through AnkiConnect's model actions was the
alternative and is rejected in ADR-0005: the tool cannot tell a half-built
note type from one its owner changed on purpose, and rewriting the first
kind would silently discard the second.

Refs #3.

entry.title: Build a lesson's card and send it to Anki
entry.content:
Build a lesson's card and send it to Anki

Add the middle and the last stage. Build reads a lesson's Markdown and
emits the note it would create as JSON, touching nothing: the dialogue
with every Key Vocabulary term it carries blanked, the glossary from both
tables, the note type's six fields in order, and the dialogue audio under
its source filename. Import sends that note to a running Anki through
AnkiConnect, checking the EnglishPod deck is there, making the EnglishPod
Cloze note type when the collection lacks it, and uploading the audio
before the note that plays it.

Matching normalises three things and no more: the page's line wrapping, so
a term split across lines still matches; simple inflections, so `plunge`
finds `plunged`, `govern` finds `governing` and `road trip` finds `road
trips`; and bracketed annotations, so `(be) overstocked` is `overstocked`.
Every occurrence of a term is blanked, not only the first. Measured against
the 191 lessons already preprocessed that places 87.6% of Key Vocabulary
terms, around 8.4 blanks a lesson, and reports the rest -- `chapter elven`
where the dialogue says `eleven`, `quality control` where it says `QC`,
`write off` where the dialogue has `write them off`. Those want a human eye
rather than a fuzzy match, which is what ADR-0003 asks for.

A note cannot be given a guid through AnkiConnect, so it is born with a tag
carrying the lesson code, `englishpod::C0108`, which is what a later run
searches for to find what an earlier one made. ADR-0004 records why a tag
rather than a field or a file.

The lesson model and its Markdown form move to lesson.py, the one shape the
stages meet on, along with the rule about what a lesson directory holds.
That leaves card.py reading Markdown and never a PDF, as the design
requires, and the two discovery rules preprocess and build were about to
each write for themselves in one place.

Tested through the command line against a stub AnkiConnect that records
what it was asked to do, so no test needs Anki, the network or a corpus.
The lesson directory fixture gains the dialogue audio it always should have
had; the build tests read a Markdown lesson written to exercise a wrapped
term, an inflected one, a bracketed one and one the dialogue never carries.

Closes #3.

entry.title: Correct the Dialogue glossary entry on speaker labels
entry.content:
Correct the Dialogue glossary entry on speaker labels

The entry claimed speakers are always labelled `A:`/`B:`. Measured across
the 230 lesson PDFs that have a text layer, that holds for only 165 of
them: 32 add a `C:`, six add `C:` and `D:`, and the rest name their
speakers (`Steven:`, `Team A:`, `HUSBAND:`).

The entry now defines a speaker label by its shape, which is what the
parser accepts, and no longer states a claim the corpus contradicts.

entry.title: Decide line-break hyphens with the dictionary
entry.content:
Decide line-break hyphens with the dictionary

A word the typesetter broke over a line and a hyphen the author typed are
identical on the page, so no rule about where the break sits can tell them
apart. The old rule removed every hyphen, which turned `non-variable` into
`nonvariable` and `government-run` into `governmentrun`.

Ask the dictionary instead: close the word up when it knows the result,
otherwise keep the hyphen. The offline dictionary is cmudict, which the
pronunciation stage needs anyway. It was picked by measurement against the
corpus -- 37/37 on a hand-built set of real cases, against 36/37 for the
system word list and 25/37 for hunspell, which lacks inflections.

A word the dictionary does not know keeps its hyphen rather than have one
guessed away. That leaves roughly fifteen rare words hyphenated across a
break; ~1250 joins are healed.

Reading the words back out needed two fixes found by the same measurement:
`use_text_flow` keeps a wide speaker label whole where it overlaps the word
after it, and a possessive ending in an apostrophe no longer swallows the
word in front of it.

Refs #2.

entry.title: Preprocess a lesson PDF into Markdown
entry.content:
Preprocess a lesson PDF into Markdown

Add the command-line entry point with its three subcommands, and the
preprocess stage, which reads a lesson directory's PDF and writes a
Markdown file beside it: the lesson code read from inside the PDF, the
dialogue with its speaker labels and physical line structure, and the
Key and Supplementary Vocabulary tables.

The vocabulary tables' column geometry differs between the corpus's two
layout families, so it is recovered per table from the gaps that stay
empty down the whole table, rather than hard-coded.

The sample lessons the tests run against are drawn from scratch, copying
the geometry of a real lesson PDF without copying any of the corpus,
which is copyrighted.

Refs #2.

entry.title: Add domain glossary and design decisions
entry.content:
Add domain glossary and design decisions

CONTEXT.md records the language this project speaks: lesson, lesson
code, dialogue, Key Vocabulary, Supplementary Vocabulary, cloze blank,
glossary, lesson card, skipped lesson.

The three ADRs capture decisions from the design interview that a
future reader would otherwise re-litigate, each with the alternative
that was rejected:

- 0001  import through AnkiConnect rather than a generated .apkg
- 0002  convert PDFs to reviewable Markdown before building cards
- 0003  one cloze card per lesson, blanks drawn from Key Vocabulary,
        matching the shape of the hand-built card for lesson 108
